lectori-f3.text: Si me commorit, melius non tangere clamo. Hor

translations.literal: If he shall have stirred me up, 'better not to touch,' I shout.
translations.note: Horace, Satires 2.1.44–46: 'at ille, / qui me commorit (melius non tangere, clamo), / flebit' ('but whoever provokes me, better not touch me, I cry, will weep for it'). Burton writes 'Si' for Horace's 'qui' and leaves out the following 'flebit' ('will weep'). The sidenote supports the threat in the main text that Democritus Junior will turn a hostile critic into a joke.
translations.text: If he provokes me, 'Better not touch!' I cry.

lectori-f6.text: Damageto, accersitus sum ut Democritum tanquam insanum curarem, sed postquam conveni non per Jovem desipientiae negotium, sed rerum omnium receptaculum deprehendi, ejusque ingenium demiratus sum

translations.literal: To Damagetus, I was summoned that I might cure Democritus as if insane, but after I met him I found not, by Jove, a business of foolishness, but a receptacle of all things, and I wondered at his intellect
translations.note: Damageto is a dative of address, the heading of a letter. The words come from the pseudo-Hippocratic letters about Democritus and the people of Abdera, in which Hippocrates writes to his friend Damagetus. Burton's Latin reads as a condensed summary of that letter, not a word-for-word quotation. The sentence that follows in the sidenote, outside this passage, says that Hippocrates instead blamed the Abderites, who needed hellebore more than Democritus did.
translations.text: To Damagetus: I was summoned to cure Democritus as a madman, but after I had met him I found, by Jupiter, no case of folly but a storehouse of all things, and I marvelled at his genius
